opus-5.5.text:
Oh, I think it's a wonderful resource, honestly. Erdős left behind this enormous collection of problems, hundreds and hundreds of them, scattered across papers, talks, letters, and lectures over decades. For a long time there wasn't one place where you could see them all and ask, "What's the current status of this one? Is it solved? Partially solved? Still wide open?" Thomas Bloom took on the very unglamorous but incredibly important work of collecting them, stating them carefully, and keeping track of progress.

What I find most valuable is that it turns this folklore into something structured. You have a clean statement, references, and comments from the community. That matters a lot for mathematicians, but it also turned out to matter for AI. When we started seeing models like GPT-5 help with research-level math, one natural question was: can these models actually locate or contribute something on real open problems? Having a well-curated list with clear statuses gave a concrete place to test that.

And one of the interesting lessons was that a lot of "open" problems on the list turned out to already have solutions somewhere in the literature, just buried in some paper nobody connected to the original question. The models were surprisingly good at that kind of deep literature search, finding the link between a problem and an obscure result. So the website became a meeting point between humans and AI, where both could contribute and the record gets corrected and improved. I think that's a model for how this kind of collaboration should work: transparent, carefully curated, and with experts like Thomas checking what's real.

r001.rationale: The response says some problems listed as open had already been solved in the literature, with solutions buried in obscure papers.

r002.rationale: It describes the curated list as a concrete place to test whether models can locate or contribute to real open problems in research-level mathematics.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing is just that it exists. Erdős left behind something like a thousand problems scattered across decades of papers, and before Thomas put this site together there was no single place where you could go and ask, "okay, which of these are still open, which have been solved, and what's the current state of play?" That's a huge service to the community on its own.

But the thing I find really valuable, especially from where I sit, is that it's a curated collection of problems that are genuinely well-posed, hard, and have a known status. That's exactly what you want when you're trying to understand what these AI systems can actually do in mathematics. You don't want benchmark problems that someone made up last week. You want problems that a brilliant mathematician thought were interesting, that real people have spent time on, and where there's a clear notion of what "solved" means. The Erdős problems database gives you that, and Thomas has been very careful about documenting the literature around each one.

And there's a nice feedback loop happening too. When a model finds something, say it turns out a problem was actually resolved in a paper from the eighties that nobody connected to Erdős's formulation, Thomas updates the site. So the database itself gets better, and it becomes a kind of shared ground truth between the mathematicians and the people building these systems. I think that's the healthy way for this to go, where the tools and the human experts are both contributing to the same record.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a problem may have been resolved in an older paper without being connected to Erdős’s formulation, and that Thomas updates the site when this is found.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes the collection as valuable for understanding what AI systems can do in mathematics, using hard, well-posed problems with known status.

astra-6.text: What I find valuable is that it makes the frontier very concrete. You can look at a problem, see whether it’s open, and understand what progress has been made. Having that information collected in one place is incredibly useful: it helps you find questions to work on and puts individual results in context. And if you’re interested in whether AI can contribute to mathematics, it gives you concrete problems to ask about—can it actually help us make progress on something we don’t know how to solve?

sol-6.1.text: What I find valuable is that it makes the frontier very concrete. You can look at a problem, see whether it’s open or solved, and follow the discussion around it. Instead of mathematics feeling like this enormous, inaccessible body of knowledge, you have specific questions you can engage with. And for thinking about AI doing mathematics, that’s especially useful: these are questions people actually care about, with a history behind them.
